item.title: Equity Index Types: Broad, Multi-Market, Sector and Style
item.summary: Equity indexes come in families that differ in which slice of the stock market they track: a whole market, several countries, one industry, or one investing style. Knowing the families helps you pick a sensible yardstick for a portfolio and read what an index number says.

sections.heading: Why different index types exist
sections.body_markdown: An **equity index** is a rule-based basket of shares whose combined value is tracked over time, like a thermometer for a part of the market. A single thermometer cannot describe every room, so providers build indexes that cover different slices. The four families you need are **broad market**, **multi-market**, **sector** and **style**. They are not rival categories. They answer different questions: how much of the market is covered, where the companies are listed, which industry they belong to, and what kind of stock they are.

sections.heading: Broad market and multi-market indexes
sections.body_markdown: A **broad market index** covers a very large share of the listed shares in one market, across many industries and company sizes. It is meant to stand for that market's overall performance. A **multi-market index** gathers shares from several countries. It may be global, regional (for example, Europe), or limited to a group such as developed or emerging markets. The first idea is about *coverage of one market*. The second is about *geographic reach*. Index providers also build narrower versions, such as large-cap-only indexes, from the same universe.

sections.heading: Sector indexes
sections.body_markdown: A **sector index** holds only companies from one industry group, such as financials, health care, energy or utilities. Providers assign each company to a sector using a classification scheme (GICS and ICB are common). Sector indexes show how one part of the economy is doing and act as benchmarks for sector funds. They are also useful for comparing sectors that behave differently over the business cycle. Cyclical sectors, such as consumer discretionary, swing with the economy. Defensive sectors, such as utilities, tend to be steadier. A sector index can also be multi-market, for example a global health care index, so the labels overlap.

sections.heading: Style indexes
sections.body_markdown: A **style index** groups stocks by investing characteristics, mainly **size** (large, mid, small market capitalization) and **value versus growth**. *Value* stocks look cheap against fundamentals, with a high book-to-price ratio, a low price-to-earnings ratio or a high dividend yield. *Growth* stocks have strong expected or past growth in sales and earnings. Stocks in between are often called *blend* or *core*. Size and value/growth are often combined, giving labels like small-cap value or large-cap growth. Some providers do not force each stock into one box. Russell scores each stock on a book-to-price measure and growth measures, then assigns part of its weight to the value index and the rest to the growth index, so the two always add to 100% (before capping). Providers also offer other characteristic-based indexes, such as Russell's defensive (stable) and dynamic indexes, which draw on earnings variability, leverage, ROA and price volatility. Style indexes are the natural benchmark for a fund that follows a particular style.

worked_example.problem: A study group lists four indexes: (1) an index of nearly all listed shares in one country, spanning every industry and company size; (2) an index of shares from developed and emerging markets worldwide; (3) an index of only utility companies listed in one country; (4) an index of the smallest listed companies in one country that have high book-to-price ratios. Classify each index.
steps: Index 1: it covers a very large share of one market and many industries, so it is a broad market index.
Index 2: it draws on shares from many countries, so it is a multi-market index. Geography is the defining feature.
Index 3: it contains one industry group only, so it is a sector index. Being limited to one country does not change that.
Index 4: it is chosen by company size (small) and by a valuation characteristic (high book-to-price means value), so it is a style index, specifically small-cap value.
Check overlap: a global utilities index would be both a sector index and a multi-market index, so the labels are not mutually exclusive.
worked_example.answer: 1 = broad market; 2 = multi-market; 3 = sector; 4 = style (small-cap value).

exam_traps: Confusing broad market with multi-market. Broad means wide coverage of one market. Multi-market means shares from several countries.
Treating value stocks as having a high price-to-book. Value stocks typically have a low price-to-book, which is the same as a high book-to-price.
Assuming every stock sits in exactly one style bucket. Some providers split a stock between the value and growth indexes in proportions that sum to 100%.
Assuming sector and multi-market are mutually exclusive. A global sector index is both.
Calling a sector index a diversified measure of the whole market. It holds one industry group and can differ sharply from the market.
builds_on: What a stock market index is
Valuation ratios such as book-to-price and P/E

item.stem: An index is built from a large proportion of all the listed shares in one country, covering many industries and company sizes. Which type of equity index is this?

options.text: Sector index
options.explanation: A sector index would hold only one industry group, but this index spans many industries.

options.text: Broad market index
options.explanation: Correct. Wide coverage of a single market across industries and sizes defines a broad market index.

options.text: Style index
options.explanation: A style index picks stocks by size or value/growth traits, not by covering most of the market.

item.stem: An index contains large companies listed in many different countries, both developed and emerging. Which type of equity index is this?

options.text: Broad market index covering one country
options.explanation: That would be limited to one country's market, whereas this index spans many countries.

options.text: Style index based on book-to-price
options.explanation: Nothing in the description sorts stocks by value or growth traits; the defining feature is geography.

options.text: Multi-market index covering several countries
options.explanation: Correct. An index drawing shares from several countries is a multi-market index.

item.stem: A fund invests only in banks and insurers listed in one country. Which index type is the most natural benchmark?

options.text: A sector index for financial companies
options.explanation: Correct. The fund is defined by industry, so a sector index of financial companies matches it.

options.text: A multi-market index of global shares
options.explanation: This confuses geography with industry. The fund is single-country and industry-focused.

options.text: A broad market index of the country
options.explanation: It would include many unrelated industries, so it would not match the fund's narrow exposure.

item.stem: Compared with the overall market, which characteristic is typical of stocks placed in a value index?

options.text: A higher forecast earnings growth rate
options.explanation: This describes growth stocks, so it mixes up the two styles.

options.text: A higher book-to-price ratio
options.explanation: Correct. Value stocks trade cheaply against book value, which means a high book-to-price ratio.

options.text: A lower dividend yield
options.explanation: Value stocks tend to have higher dividend yields, so a lower yield points the wrong way.

item.stem: An index provider scores stocks on book-to-price and growth measures and splits each stock between its value and growth indexes. Before any weight capping, a stock receives a 20% weight in the value index. What weight does it receive in the matching growth index?

options.text: 20%, the same as in the value index
options.explanation: This assumes the stock gets the same weight in both indexes. The two weights must add up to 100%.

options.text: 0%, because a stock can sit in only one style index
options.explanation: This assumes a stock must be put in a single style. This method deliberately allows partial membership in both.

options.text: 80%, so the two weights add up to 100%
options.explanation: Correct. The stock is fully represented by the sum of its value and growth weights, so 100% − 20% = 80%.

item.stem: A global health care index holds companies from both developed and emerging markets. How is it best described?

options.text: Both a sector index and a multi-market index, because the labels overlap
options.explanation: Correct. It is limited to one industry (sector) and spans several countries (multi-market).

options.text: A multi-market index only, because sector indexes must be single-country
options.explanation: No such rule exists. Sector indexes can be built from one country or from many.

options.text: A sector index only, because multi-market indexes must hold every industry
options.explanation: Multi-market indexes can be restricted to one industry. Geography and industry are separate dimensions.

item.stem: A fund manager runs a portfolio of large companies with strong earnings growth. Which benchmark best fits the portfolio's style?

options.text: A broad market index of all listed shares
options.explanation: It mixes all sizes and styles, so it is a poor match for a large-cap growth portfolio.

options.text: A large-cap growth style index
options.explanation: Correct. A benchmark should share the portfolio's size and value/growth characteristics.

options.text: A sector index of the largest single sector
options.explanation: This picks one industry, but the portfolio is defined by size and growth, not by industry.

item.front: How does a broad market index differ from a multi-market index?
item.back: A broad market index covers a large share of the shares in one market. A multi-market index combines shares from several countries (global, regional, developed or emerging).

item.front: What is a sector index and what is it used for?
item.back: An index of companies from one industry group, such as financials or utilities. It shows how that part of the economy is doing and serves as a benchmark for sector-focused funds.

item.front: Which valuation traits typically mark value stocks, and which mark growth stocks?
item.back: Value stocks: high book-to-price (low P/E, often higher dividend yield). Growth stocks: strong past or expected growth in sales and earnings.

item.front: Which two dimensions do style indexes usually combine?
item.back: Size (large, mid, small cap) and value versus growth, giving labels like small-cap value or large-cap growth.
